extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and law students studying patent subject-matter and claim drafting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding whether an invention is patentable as an art (process), machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, and for how to claim and draft specifications (including improvements and combinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject-matter and pre‑grant bars
rubrics_metrics.description: That any person who has invented or discovered any "new and useful art, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof" may obtain a patent, provided the thing is "not known or used by others in this country, and not patented or described in any printed publication in this or any foreign country, before his invention or discovery thereof, and not in public use or on sale for more than two years prior to his application, unless the same is proved to have been abandoned."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language sets both the categories of patentable subject-matter (art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, and improvements) and the novelty/public‑use/on‑sale time bars. Any analysis of patentability should start from these statutory categories and the requirement that the claimed subject was not previously known, used, published, or on sale beyond the statutory grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'art' (process/method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'art' was intended to embrace inventions where apparatus or materials may not be the essence of the discovery, but where that essence consists in using apparatus or materials in new processes, methods, or relations, so as to constitute a new mode of attaining an old result; or a mode of attaining a new result; or an entirely new process of making or doing something which has not been made or done before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'art' covers novel modes of applying existing materials/apparatus (e.g., new relations/order/position of known elements). Examples include new dyeing/tanning methods and the printing-on-both-sides bank-note example (new application of letter-press and copperplate for added security). When the novelty lies in a new method of application rather than new apparatus/substance, claim as an art/process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper characterization and claiming (process vs machine/manufacture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the subject-matter of a particular patent is a process (an improvement in an art) or a new manufacture/machine/composition is often decisive; an invention that is in substance a new process but is claimed as a machine or manufacture may be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the specification and claims to reflect the essential nature of the invention. The Kay v. Marshall example shows that claiming a process invention as machinery (e.g., claiming altered placement of rollers rather than the process of maceration + short reach spinning) can doom a patent. If the real invention is a process, describe it as such (steps, sequence, conditions) to avoid losing protection by mischaracterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of a process independent of the product
rubrics_metrics.description: A process and the product of a process may be both new and patentable, and are wholly disconnected and independent of each other; patentability may exist as to either, neither, or both, according to novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty separately for the process and for any product/result. The fact that a machine is old does not preclude a new process using that machine from being patentable (e.g., spinning macerated flax on an old machine). Conversely, a new machine may produce an old product; the machine could be patentable even if the product is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a process is patentable despite product sameness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the process itself is different from the old process, it may be patentable even though the article produced may not be improved in properties; alternatively, if the article produced is improved (different or superior properties), the process is patentable as an improvement in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hall's lace singeing (application of gas flame produced superior finish — process sustained); cases where a different agency yields superior article or economic/quality benefits (Crane's hot blast with anthracite producing cheaper/better iron). Emphasize the agency/steps of the process and the effect produced when arguing process patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'machine' and when mechanism is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine is the subject of a patent when a function or mode of operation is embodied in mechanism designed to accomplish a particular effect; a machine is patentable whenever a new or an old effect is produced by mechanism new in its combinations, arrangements, or mode of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention is a function tied to particular, permanent mechanism (new combinations, arrangements, or principles of operation), claim as a machine. Courts look to whether the mechanism's principle or modus operandi is new; a machine can also be a new combination of existing machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents vs patents for parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'machine' in the statute includes new combinations of machines, as well as new organizations of mechanism for a single purpose. In such cases the thing patented is the combination, not the separate machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully draft claims to indicate whether protection is sought for the combination as a whole or for individual parts. The question of whether a claim is for a combination only or for specific parts as well is one of claim construction on the patent and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement patents (what counts as an 'improvement')
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement, applied to machinery, is where a specific machine already exists and an addition or alteration is made to produce the same effects in a better manner, or where new combinations are added to produce new effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an improvement patent, the invention must be a real and material improvement, not a mere change of form. The inquiry focuses on whether some new element, combination, or feature has been added that produces the same effect more cheaply or expeditiously, or an entirely new or materially superior effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for whether an alleged improvement operates on same principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry is whether the alleged improved machine operates upon the same principle as the former machine; i.e., whether it produces the same effect by the same mechanical means or by means which are substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine modus operandi and mechanical principles rather than superficial form. Two machines may look similar externally but operate on different principles; conversely, they may employ the same principle despite differences in form. Where effect is different, focus on the character and importance of the effect itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality/triviality of improvement is a factual question
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an improvement is trifling and insignificant, or real and important, is a question for the jury (i.e., a factual determination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating improvements, be prepared to present technical evidence on the advantage, efficiency, cost, or quality gains to show materiality; courts will not treat trivial changes as patentable improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of unskilful claim/specification construction
rubrics_metrics.description: If an inventor describes or claims the invention in an improper form (e.g., claims a machine when the real invention is a process, or vice versa), the patent may be invalid or narrower than intended. Such unskilful construction may forfeit rights to the real invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and specifications carefully to encompass the real invention. The Corning/Le Roy examples illustrate that an ambiguously constructed instrument can lead courts to construe the patent too narrowly (e.g., as a machine rather than a process), allowing defendants to introduce evidence that should otherwise be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: When process/product advantages support patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the result produced by the combination (process or machine) is a new article, a better article, or a cheaper article to the public than produced before by the old method, that combination is an invention or manufacture intended by the statute and may be the subject of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to advantages such as superior finish, better properties, increased yield, lower cost, or lasting effect (examples: lace singeing for superior finish; paper glazing for improved fine-line reproduction; successive immersion to render fabrics water-proof yet air‑pervious). Emphasize the public utility and tangible advantages obtained by the new process or machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patenting an improvement on an existing patent
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a patent for an improvement of a machine that is itself the subject of an existing patent; a patent including the subject-matter of a patent still in force is valid if the improvement only is claimed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improvement patent can coexist with an earlier patent covering the base machine, but practical enforcement may be subject to expiration timing, licensing, or purchase of the original patented machine. When prosecuting improvement claims, confine claims to the improvement to avoid invalidity for double-patenting or overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of distinguishing process and product when preparing specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A careful discrimination between an improved process and an improved machine, manufacture, or composition of matter is essential when preparing a specification; the discrimination must be guided by the nature of the invention and its essential character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before drafting, analyze whether novelty lies in (a) the agency/steps (process), (b) the apparatus/principle (machine), or (c) the article's properties (manufacture/composition). If both process and product are novel, consider claiming both, with directions enabling construction of suitable machinery where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction rule to secure the real invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The general rule of construction is that the real invention is to be beneficially secured to the patentee, if the terms of his specification will admit of it; hence construction of claims will aim to give effect to the inventor's real discovery within the words used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will construe claims to secure the inventor's real invention when the specification's language permits. Nevertheless, sloppy or ambiguous claim language that ties novelty improperly (e.g., to a particular apparatus instead of the process) risks narrowing protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples as illustrative guidance (use of prior cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete cases illustrate application of these principles: printing bank-notes by printing on both sides (new application of old materials = art); spinning macerated flax (process vs machine claim failure when misclaimed); casting iron rollers by imparting rotary motion (novel mode); Crane's hot blast with anthracite producing cheaper/better iron (process/manufacture interplay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case examples as templates when analyzing analogous inventions: identify whether novelty is in steps/agency, apparatus principle, combination, or resulting properties; map the facts to precedent to decide claim scope and drafting strategy.
